muc.title: Picking up from LiDAR
muc.text: Part 1, video 5 on LiDAR, measured the road in three steps: fire a laser pulse, start the clock, work out the distance. But in thick fog, water droplets scatter the laser everywhere, and the car needs a second eye: radar.

muc.title: Long waves slip through fog
muc.text: Radar measures distance with radio waves. The waves used in cars are almost 4 mm long, about 4,300 times longer than LiDAR's laser. Fog droplets are far smaller than that, so the waves slip right through.

muc.title: The same three steps as LiDAR
muc.text: Radar follows exactly the same three steps as LiDAR: send a wave, time it, work out the distance. For a car 150 meters ahead, the round trip takes just one millionth of a second.

muc.title: Doppler measures speed
muc.text: Radar's big advantage is measuring speed instantly, thanks to the Doppler effect. Just as an ambulance siren sounds higher as it comes closer, waves bouncing off an approaching object get squeezed together. If the car ahead is 10 meters per second slower, the wave shifts by about 5,000 hertz.

muc.title: Blurry, and easily fooled
muc.text: The trade-off: radar sees very blurrily, so it struggles to tell a person from a motorbike or a sign. Metal reflects very strongly, so a can or an overpass can be mistaken for an obstacle.

muc.title: Radar is everywhere
muc.text: Radar powers adaptive cruise control, blind-spot warnings and weather rain maps.

muc.title: Look at rain radar
muc.text: Open the rain map in your weather app and pick the radar layer. The green, yellow and red patches are waves bouncing back off raindrops, showing whether rain is about to reach you.
